cards.title: Venezuela American Oil Deal
cards.script:
![[https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp](https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp)](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013451578-ei0v.jpg)

Will the US take over of Venezuelan oil fields lower gas prices? Let's take a look.

![](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013236533-38vp.jpg)

Historically, Venezuela produced around 2.5 mbd. But since the crash in oil prices are the end of 2014 and the gross mismanagement of the Maduro administration, production has fallen to around 1 mbd. - so we are looking at an increase of 1-2 mbd.

![[https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/images/Fig2.png](https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/images/Fig2.png)](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013238685-pa34.jpg)

Now let's compare to global output. Before the war, the globe produced around 105 mbd, the latest data shows that fell to 95 - a gap of ten.

I don't think we need any fancy math to know that two is smaller than ten.

But there are other issues.

1. It will take years of capital investment to get production back up to historical levels.

The second is a lot more interesting. Trump appears to be our most socialist president ever. This new supposed deal in Venezuela places the U.S. government as a majority shareholder.

![[https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp](https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/trump-administration-in-advanced-talks-for-stake-in-venezuelan-oil-fields-819546d3?mod=mhp)](data/images/cwmihqah-1788013942776-49d1.jpg)

While defining capitalism and socialism can involve a lot of variables, my simple one sentence version is, "Who owns the means of production?"

We're seeing a broader trend by the current administration. A move towards more state ownership of the means of production. The government now has stakes in [30 different firms](https://www.cato.org/blog/government-ownership-stakes-companies-becoming-routine-under-trump).

The arguments in favor - an argument repeated by socialists, such as Bernie Sanders, note that the Federal Government often gives favorable tax breaks or grants to businesses without any return back to the government. That is beyond the general macroeconomic improvements these policies are designed for. Instead, if the government owns stocks, it would then share in some of the profits.

Well, why haven't we been doing this all along? We can point to 150 years years of attempts to make these arrangements work.

As Giacomo Corneo points out in his excellent book, "Is Capitalism Obsolete? A Journey Through Alternative Economic Systems"

"Sometimes state involvement has worked, and sometimes it has not. Typically it has not when governments imposed business decisions on management and misused enterprises under their control for party-political ends."

Government ownership changes the incentive structure. Rather than consumers and other business competitors disciplining a firm to operate efficiently, firms specialize in pleasing government leaders to receive profits.

The consumers end up worse. Inefficient and cost burdened firms are propped up longer than they should. We get waste instead of winning.

cards.title: Colorado River Allocation
cards.script:
![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787850366846-c3j9.png)

Is capitalism to blame for the overuse of the Colorado River?

Afterall, profits mean water extraction.

Golf courses in the desert. High rise condos. Sprawling Metropolises.

However, there's just one problem with this narrative - The Colorado River is not run by the unadulterated free market.

It's central planning with feudal characteristics.

Here's what I mean.

1. There's no real functioning water market.  Yes, there's some markets for temporary leasing inside a state. But you can't plan big long-term projects like that.

The government decided 150 years ago how much water a particular plot of land can extract. And those - now practically ancient - water claims keep getting past down from generation to generation like the feudal lords of old.

2. Unlike other assets in capitalism, it's use it or lose it. No incentive for thriftiness or storing for the future.

Result: the classic soviet-style waste you get from central planning.

But wait, it sounds like we're talking about large tracts of land and farming. Aren't the big cities and the 40 million people relying on the Colorado River the real ones to blame?

No. Here is the sources and uses of the Colorado River.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787843787982-roqu.png)

Most the water enters in the Upper Basin largely through snowmelt from the Rockies.

Now, look at MCI: Municipal, Commercial, and Industrial use. It's a very small share compared to agriculture. And that agriculture is largely devoted to growing alfalfa and hay, an incredibly low-value cash crop.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787850314567-m1k6.png)

It's not just the Colorado. The Great Salt Lake Basin shows a similar pattern.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1788374785590-g3u7.jpg)

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1788382858129-4o6k.png)

The Salt Lake is declining every decade. Lakes Powell and Mead are now near record lows.

It's [estimated](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024002312) that we need to reduce water use by more than 25% just to stabilize the reservoirs.

So, where should the cuts happen?

If you ask an economist - we'd say the lowest value activity.

And...markets are a pretty great way to reveal that information.

We've already done this. It's how we solved the Acid Rain problem back in the 90's.

We need a "cap and trade" for the Colorado and Great Salt Lake.

Today, farmers profits are boosted on the backs of working families. Farmers pay on avg $30 per acre foot compared to the $512 dollars the rest of us pay.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787839527433-2ecs.jpg)

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787839529928-4pt1.jpg)

We call this rent seeking. Earning profits not because you produce what society values most, but because you force society to give you more than what you produce. If you can't pay the real costs - you shouldn't be producing it.

In The Great Salt Lake Basin, hay and alfalfa only contribute 0.07% to the economy.

![[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024002312](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667010024002312)](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1788385475061-bwa9.png)

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849131550-qpuw.jpg)

What if we just paid the farmers off? It would be less than an annual Netflix subscription per person. But I gotta be honest, it's sits uneasy that in perpetuity, farmers and their descendants get free cash from the public, just cuz of some great great grandad.

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849133071-jrkt.jpg)

The debate is about cultural issues, not economics or food security. It's the lifestyles of the 20k farmers and ranchers in the basin. That is, in a region of 2.8M, why are we giving out cultural sympathy points to businesses that produce a low value product?

![](data/images/ciwg4e7t-1787849134938-vvr4.jpg)

That ain't capitalism.

We need more well regulated water markets, not historical feudal water claims. The Salt Lake and Colorado River Basins can support cities two or even three times as large, doubling the economy. All while preserving even more water for environmental needs.

Note: this video was 3:33 minutes long after recording.
